prompt: What has to be on `web1` for Ana's laptop to configure it with Ansible?
hint: Look at what the lesson says Ubuntu already ships.

choices.text: An Ansible agent registered with a central server
choices.why: That is the picture the lesson corrects: Ansible pushes from the laptop and has no agent.

choices.text: A copy of the inventory and the playbook
choices.why: Both stay on the control node; the machine only receives small programs while a command runs.

choices.text: An SSH server and Python
choices.why: Yes. Ansible logs in over SSH and runs modules written in Python; nothing else is installed.

choices.text: Ansible itself, at the same version as the laptop's
choices.why: Ansible is installed once, on the control node, and never on the machines it manages.

prompt: `ansible db1 -m ping` comes back as `UNREACHABLE!`. What does that tell Ana?
hint: Compare it with FAILED.

choices.text: The module ran and returned an error
choices.why: That would be FAILED: logged in, and the task went wrong.

choices.text: Ansible never managed to log in
choices.why: Right. In the lesson it was SSH refusing `root`, whose key is not authorised; no module ran at all.

choices.text: The machine does not answer ICMP echo requests from the laptop
choices.why: Ansible's `ping` is a module run over SSH, not the network ping.

choices.text: `db1` is missing from the inventory
choices.why: A host the inventory does not have matches nothing; Ansible would not try to reach it at all.

prompt: Match each line of Ana's `inventory.ini` to what it does.
hint: A name in brackets is not a host.

prompt: Ana runs `ansible web -m apt -a "name=tree state=present" --become` a second time, right after the first. What does each host report?
hint: The module looks before it acts.

choices.text: CHANGED, because apt-get install ran again on the machine
choices.why: That is what `command` would report. `apt` checks first and installs nothing when the package is there.

choices.text: FAILED, because the package already exists
choices.why: A state that is already true is a success, not an error.

choices.text: UNREACHABLE, until the cache is refreshed
choices.why: UNREACHABLE is about logging in; the cache has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: SUCCESS with `"changed": false`
choices.why: Yes. The package is present, so the module did nothing and says so.

prompt: `ansible web1 -m command -a "dpkg -l | grep -c ^ii"` fails, and the same text with `-m shell` prints a number. Why?
hint: Who interprets the `|`?

choices.text: `command` runs the program with no shell, so the pipe became arguments to `dpkg`
choices.why: Right. dpkg received `|`, `grep`, `-c` and `^ii` as package names.

choices.text: `command` needs `--become` to read the package list
choices.why: Listing packages needs no root; `shell` ran without `--become` too.

choices.text: grep is not installed on web1
choices.why: It is; the failed output even lists the package `grep`.

choices.text: Ad-hoc commands accept one word
choices.why: `tree --version` worked with `command`; it takes several arguments.

prompt: Why does `ansible web1 -m command -a "tree --version"` report CHANGED, when it only printed a version?
hint: What can `command` know about the program it ran?

choices.text: Printing a version updates apt's cache
choices.why: Nothing on the machine changed; the report comes from what the module can know.

choices.text: It cannot tell
choices.why: Yes. `command` runs a program and cannot see what it did, so it assumes a change every time.

choices.text: The first run of any module on a host is reported as a change
choices.why: `ping` reported `"changed": false` on its first run, and `command` reports CHANGED on every run.

choices.text: Ad-hoc commands always report CHANGED, unlike playbooks
choices.why: The second `apt` ad-hoc command reported SUCCESS; it depends on the module, not on how it is run.

prompt: The first run of `site.yml` ends with `web1 : ok=5 changed=4`. How should Ana read the two numbers?
hint: One of them contains the other.

choices.text: Nine tasks ran: five fine and four that changed
choices.why: The counts overlap: `ok` includes every successful task, changed or not.

choices.text: Five tasks succeeded and four of them changed something
choices.why: Right. The fifth, gathering facts, changed nothing.

choices.text: Four tasks still need a second run
choices.why: A change is something done, not something pending; the second run reported changed=0.

choices.text: Four warnings
choices.why: `changed` counts tasks that altered the machine; warnings are not counted in the recap.

prompt: Put what `ansible-playbook site.yml` printed on its first run in order.
hint: One task nobody wrote comes first.
trap: Gathering Facts runs before the first task in the file, and the recap is always last.

prompt: A playbook has five tasks. On `web2` the third one fails; on `web1` everything succeeds. What is the state of `web2` afterwards?
hint: Ansible keeps no state to roll back to.

choices.text: As before the run, because the play rolls web2 back
choices.why: Nothing is rolled back; what tasks one and two did stays done.

choices.text: Fully configured, because web1 finished the play for both
choices.why: Each host is configured on its own; web1 succeeding does nothing to web2.

choices.text: Tasks one and two applied, three to five not
choices.why: Right. The failing host stops where it failed, and the next run starts from the top and finds the first two already true.

choices.text: Unchanged, since a failed host is skipped from the start
choices.why: Ansible cannot know a task will fail before running it; the earlier tasks ran.

prompt: A colleague edited `index.html` on `web1` by hand. Ana runs `site.yml` with nothing new in it. What happens?
hint: Look at the recap after the edit.

choices.text: The page is put back on web1 and web2 is left alone
choices.why: Yes: changed=1 on web1, changed=0 on web2.

choices.text: Nothing, because the playbook did not change
choices.why: Ansible compares with the machine, not with the last run; the machine changed.

choices.text: The page is rewritten on both web servers
choices.why: web2's page already matched, so its task reported ok.

choices.text: The run fails, reporting drift on web1
choices.why: A difference is not an error; the task corrects it and reports changed.

prompt: A task runs `nginx -t` with `ansible.builtin.command`. Why does the lesson add `changed_when: false`?
hint: What does a recap that is never zero cost?

choices.text: To stop the task from running on the second run
choices.why: It still runs every time; only what it reports changes. Skipping is what `creates` does.

choices.text: To keep the run from failing when the configuration is wrong
choices.why: That would be `failed_when`; a wrong configuration should still fail the check.

choices.text: So the recap shows real changes
choices.why: Right. A task that always says changed hides the changes that matter.

choices.text: Because `nginx -t` modifies the configuration file
choices.why: It only reads and tests it; that is exactly why reporting a change is wrong.

prompt: A `command` task that makes `/etc/ssl/certs/shop.crt` is skipped on later runs once that file exists, because the task names it with the argument ___.
hint: A verb in the third person.

prompt: Ana deletes the `Write the index page` task from `site.yml` and runs it. What happens to `/var/www/html/index.html` on the web servers?
hint: Is there a record of what Ansible made?

choices.text: It is deleted, as Terraform would destroy a removed resource
choices.why: Terraform can because its state lists what it made; Ansible has no such list.

choices.text: It stays as it is
choices.why: Right. Ansible only checks what the playbook mentions; to remove it you write a task with `state: absent`.

choices.text: The run fails because the file is no longer managed
choices.why: An unmanaged file is invisible to the run, not an error.

choices.text: It is emptied on the next run with `--check`
choices.why: `--check` changes nothing at all, and nothing mentions the file any more.

prompt: When does the `Reload nginx` handler run?
hint: Compare the runs before and after the variable changed.

choices.text: After every task that notifies it, immediately
choices.why: Handlers wait for the end of the play, and run once however many tasks notified them.

choices.text: On every run, after the last task
choices.why: The run that followed, with nothing new, had no handler at all: nothing notified it.

choices.text: At the end of the play, if a notifying task changed
choices.why: Yes. The configuration task reported changed, and the reload followed after every task.

choices.text: Only when nginx is not running
choices.why: Starting a stopped nginx is the `Start nginx` task's job.

prompt: Ana adds `www.shop.example.com` to `shop_server_name` in `group_vars/web.yml` and runs `site.yml --diff`. How many changes does the recap report for `web1`?
hint: Count the template and what it notified.

prompt: The index page template contains `{{ inventory_hostname }}`, and nobody declared that variable. Where does it come from?
hint: web1 and web2 served different pages.

choices.text: Ansible sets it: the host's name as the inventory spells it
choices.why: Right, which is why each host rendered its own page from one template.

choices.text: From `group_vars/web.yml`
choices.why: That file sets only `shop_server_name` and `shop_root`.

choices.text: From the machine's `/etc/hostname`, read by Jinja2
choices.why: Templates are rendered on the control node, and the value is the inventory's name, not the machine's.

choices.text: It is an environment variable on the laptop
choices.why: Nothing in Ana's shell sets it; Ansible provides it per host.

prompt: Each place sets `shop_server_name` to a different value. Match each to its rank, 1 being the weakest.
hint: The lesson lists them from weakest to strongest.

prompt: In a role, which directory holds variables the caller is expected to override?
hint: The weakest place of all.

choices.text: `vars/`
choices.why: `vars` wins over inventory and group variables, so a caller cannot easily override it.

choices.text: `meta/`
choices.why: `meta` holds the author, platforms and dependencies, not variables.

choices.text: `files/`
choices.why: `files` holds files copied as they are.

choices.text: `defaults/`
choices.why: Yes. Defaults lose to almost everything, which is what makes them overridable.

prompt: After moving everything into the `web` role, Ana runs `site.yml` and gets `changed=0`. What does that prove?
hint: What would a mistake in the move have done to the machines?

choices.text: The role was never used
choices.why: The tasks are named `web : Install nginx`, so they came from the role.

choices.text: That the move describes the same machines as before
choices.why: Right. A task that now rendered something different would have reported changed.

choices.text: That the role's defaults won over `group_vars/web.yml`
choices.why: The opposite: the default lacks `www`; had it won, the file would have changed.

choices.text: That the machines were replaced by new ones
choices.why: New machines would have needed nginx installed: many changes, not zero.

prompt: Which of these does `ansible-galaxy role init --init-path roles web` create? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the tree it printed.

choices.text: `roles/web/tasks/main.yml`
choices.why: Yes, the role's tasks.

choices.text: `roles/web/inventory.ini`
choices.why: A role knows nothing of which hosts it runs on; the inventory belongs to the project.

choices.text: `roles/web/handlers/main.yml`
choices.why: Yes, the role's handlers.

choices.text: `roles/web/defaults/main.yml`
choices.why: Yes, the role's default variables.

choices.text: `roles/web/site.yml`
choices.why: The playbook stays outside and names the role.

prompt: In the lesson's handover, what do Terraform and Ansible share?
hint: Neither tool knows the other exists.

choices.text: The state file, which Ansible reads to find the hosts
choices.why: Ansible never reads Terraform's state in the lesson.

choices.text: A provisioner that runs the playbook at creation
choices.why: That alternative is named and set aside: it runs once and never again.

choices.text: `hosts.ini`
choices.why: Yes. Terraform writes it with `local_file`, Ansible reads it with `-i`.

choices.text: An SSH connection opened by Terraform
choices.why: Terraform opens no connection to the machines here; Ansible does.

prompt: Why does `~/shop/infra` take the machines' addresses as a variable instead of reading them from `aws_instance` resources?
hint: What is moto, and what is it not?

choices.text: `local_file` cannot read attributes of other resources
choices.why: Any argument can reference another resource; `templatefile` would take them just the same.

choices.text: Moto runs no machines
choices.why: Right. An instance moto creates has no address anything answers on, so the containers' addresses are given instead.

choices.text: Private addresses must never be written into a file
choices.why: The inventory is exactly such a file, and that is fine.

choices.text: Ansible refuses addresses that Terraform computed
choices.why: Ansible cannot tell where a line in the inventory came from.

prompt: In `hosts.ini`, the line is `web1 ansible_host=172.30.0.11`. Which name appears in the PLAY RECAP?
hint: One name is for people, the other for SSH.

choices.why: The address is only where the connection goes.

choices.text: `web1`
choices.why: Yes. The host keeps its inventory name everywhere in Ansible; `ansible_host` changes only the connection.
The user and address are connection details, not the host's name.

choices.text: `local_file.inventory`
choices.why: That is the Terraform resource that wrote the file.

prompt: The machines are rebuilt every week by Terraform with new addresses, and Ana keeps `inventory.ini` up to date by hand. What goes wrong first?
hint: Who knows the new addresses?

choices.text: Ansible refuses to run against hosts it saw before
choices.why: Ansible keeps no memory of hosts between runs.

choices.text: Terraform plans to destroy the inventory file
choices.why: A file written by hand is not in Terraform's state at all.

choices.text: The file goes stale after a rebuild, silently
choices.why: Right. Only the tool that created the machines knows the addresses; the lesson has it write the file.

choices.text: The new machines lack Python, so every task fails
choices.why: Ubuntu ships Python; the problem is reaching the right machine at all.

prompt: A role's task runs `systemctl reload nginx` with `command` on every run. The recap is never zero. What is the fix the lesson points to?
hint: When should a reload happen at all?

choices.text: Add `changed_when: false` to the task
choices.why: The recap would read zero, but nginx would still be reloaded every run: the report becomes false instead of the work becoming right.

choices.text: A handler, notified by the configuration task
choices.why: Right. The reload then happens only when the configuration changed, and the recap tells the truth.

choices.text: Use `shell` instead of `command`
choices.why: `shell` cannot know what the program did either.

choices.text: Move the task into `vars/main.yml`
choices.why: `vars` holds variables, not tasks.

prompt: Which of these would show up in a run of Ana's `site.yml`, as written at the end of the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: The playbook checks only what it mentions.

choices.text: Someone stopped nginx on web2
choices.why: Yes: `Start nginx` would report changed on web2.

choices.text: Someone installed `htop` on web1 by hand
choices.why: No task mentions htop, so no run reports it.

choices.text: Someone edited the shop's nginx site on web1
choices.why: Yes: the template task would rewrite it and notify the reload.

choices.text: Someone added a cron job on web2
choices.why: Nothing in the role mentions cron.

choices.text: Someone deleted `/var/www/shop` on web1
choices.why: Yes: the directory task would recreate it, and the index page task would write the page again.

prompt: Put the handover from lesson 1 in order, as this lesson ran it.
hint: The file comes before anybody reads it.
items: `ssh-keyscan` trusts the machines' keys by address
trap: The host keys must be trusted before Ansible connects by address.
